lessons.title: How bash reads, expands and runs a command
lessons.goal:
Learn what bash does between you pressing Enter and a program starting: split into words, expand, then fork and exec.

Why it matters: most "weird shell behaviour" (a `*` that matches too much, a variable that splits, an error that ends up in the wrong file) is bash expanding **before** the program runs. When you can see the exact arguments a program receives, you can predict and fix these problems.

setup.note: Work in a scratch directory. Your outputs may differ in user name, PIDs and paths. The structure is the same.

steps.title: A command line is a list of words
steps.text:
Bash splits the line into **words** at blanks. The first word is the command. The other words are its arguments.

The extra blanks are not part of any word. `echo` never sees them.

steps.title: A program that shows its arguments
steps.text:
To see exactly what a program receives, we write one. `main` gets an array of strings, `argv`. This program prints every entry.

Save it as `showargs.c`, then compile it.
steps.under: A process starts with its arguments as an array of strings in memory. The kernel copies them from the `execve` call (step 8). Programs never see your original line, only this array.

steps.title: Globbing: bash expands * before the program starts
steps.text: `*.txt` is a pattern. Bash replaces it with the matching file names, sorted. The program receives the file names, not the pattern.

steps.title: Quotes stop expansion
steps.text:
Inside quotes the pattern stays a literal string. A backslash does the same for one character.

Use quotes whenever a value must reach the program unchanged.

steps.title: Variables expand too, but not in single quotes
steps.text: Double quotes allow `$name` to expand but keep the result as **one** word. Single quotes stop all expansion.

run.output:
argc = 5
argv[0] = [./showargs]
argv[1] = [hello world]
argv[2] = [hello $name]
argv[3] = [hello]
argv[4] = [world]

steps.after: The last argument has no quotes, so it expanded and then was split into two words. Unquoted expansions are split at blanks. This is the cause of many bugs with file names that contain spaces.

steps.title: Builtin or program?
steps.text: Some commands are part of bash itself (**builtins**). Others are files on disk. `type` tells you which.

run.output:
cd is a shell builtin
echo is a shell builtin
ls is hashed (/usr/bin/ls)

echo is a shell builtin
echo is /usr/bin/echo

steps.under:
`cd` must be a builtin. The working directory belongs to the process. A child process cannot change its parent's directory, so only the shell itself can do it.

`echo` exists twice: once as a builtin and once as `/usr/bin/echo`. Bash uses the builtin first.

steps.title: How bash finds a program: PATH
steps.text: For a name without a slash, bash searches the directories in `$PATH`, left to right. The current directory is not in the list, so `showargs` is not found, but `./showargs` (a path with a slash) is.
steps.after: Exit code 127 means "command not found". Code 126 means "found, but not executable".

steps.title: Underneath: fork and execve
steps.text:
Bash does not run the program itself. It creates a child process (`clone`, the system call behind `fork`). The child replaces itself with the program (`execve`). Bash waits for the child to finish.

We trace both calls and read the trace file `/tmp/trace.out`. The `*.txt` was already expanded when `execve` was called. The long number in each line is a process ID, so yours will differ.

run.output:
3357632 execve("/usr/bin/bash", ["bash", "-c", "./showargs *.txt; true"], 0xfffff3abd018 /* 54 vars */) = 0
3357632 clone(child_stack=NULL, flags=CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID|CLONE_CHILD_SETTID|SIGCHLD, child_tidptr=0xffffa013c0f0) = 3357633
3357633 execve("./showargs", ["./showargs", "a.txt", "b.txt"], 0xaaaaeceb6e50 /* 52 vars */) = 0
3357633 +++ exited with 0 +++
3357632 --- SIGCHLD {si_signo=SIGCHLD, si_code=CLD_EXITED, si_pid=3357633, si_uid=1000, si_status=0, si_utime=0, si_stime=0} ---
3357632 +++ exited with 0 +++

steps.under: `execve(path, argv, envp)` is the only way to start a program. The `argv` array you see in the trace is the same array `showargs` printed in step 3.

steps.title: Redirection: where stdout and stderr go
steps.text: Every process starts with three open files: 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout), 2 (stderr). `>` redirects 1, `2>` redirects 2, `>>` appends. Bash sets this up before it runs the command.

run.output: ls: cannot access 'nothing.txt': No such file or directory

steps.title: The order of redirections matters
steps.text:
Bash handles redirections left to right. `2>&1` means "make fd 2 point to where fd 1 points **now**".

First command: stdout goes to the file, then stderr follows it. Second command: stderr follows the terminal (still fd 1), then stdout goes to the file.

run.cmd: ls a.txt nothing.txt > both.txt 2>&1; echo '--- both.txt:'; cat both.txt
run.output:
--- both.txt:
ls: cannot access 'nothing.txt': No such file or directory
a.txt

run.cmd: ls a.txt nothing.txt 2>&1 > one.txt; echo '--- one.txt:'; cat one.txt
run.output:
ls: cannot access 'nothing.txt': No such file or directory
--- one.txt:
a.txt

steps.title: Pipes and exit codes
steps.text: `|` connects stdout of the left command to stdin of the right one. Both run at the same time. Every command ends with an exit code in `$?`: 0 means success, anything else means failure.

run.output:
ls: cannot access 'nothing.txt': No such file or directory
exit code: 2

quiz.q: You run `ls *.txt`. Who turns `*.txt` into file names?
quiz.explain: Bash expands the pattern and passes the file names to `ls` in `argv`. Step 3 showed it with `showargs`.
Double quotes allow the variable to expand but keep the result as one word.

quiz.q: Why can `cd` not be a normal program on disk?
options: A child process cannot change its parent's working directory
quiz.explain: The working directory is a per-process attribute. Only the shell process itself can change its own, so `cd` is a builtin.

quiz.q: A command prints `command not found`. Which exit code does `$?` show?
quiz.explain: 127 means not found. 126 means the file was found but cannot be executed.

quiz.q: Which command writes the error message to `file` and nothing to the terminal?
quiz.explain: Redirections run left to right. In `> file 2>&1`, fd 1 goes to the file first, then fd 2 follows it. Step 10 showed the other order.

check.scenario: A script runs `rm $file` and `$file` holds `my notes.txt`. It deletes nothing you wanted, and prints two errors about `my` and `notes.txt` not existing. Using what you learned, explain what happened and how to fix it.
check.answer:
The unquoted `$file` expanded and was **split into two words** at the blank, so `rm` received two arguments: `my` and `notes.txt`. Step 5 showed the same with `hello $name`.

Fix: quote the expansion, `rm "$file"`. Then `rm` receives one argument: `my notes.txt`.

lessons.title: Environment variables and what a child inherits
lessons.goal:
Learn the difference between a shell variable and an environment variable, and how a child process gets its environment.

Why it matters: a variable you set but did not export is invisible to every program you start. Most "it works in my shell but not in the script" problems come from this.

setup.note: Work in a scratch directory. Outputs will differ in PIDs and paths; the structure is the same.

steps.title: A shell variable stays in the shell
steps.text: `x=1` creates a **shell variable**. It lives inside the bash process only. A program started from bash does not see it.

steps.title: export puts it into the environment
steps.text: `export x` marks the variable for export. Every child started afterwards gets a copy.

steps.title: A child cannot change its parent
steps.text: The child gets a **copy**. If the child changes it, the parent never sees the change.
steps.under: The kernel copies the environment into the new process at `execve`. After that, the two processes have separate memory. There is no way for a child to write into its parent's variables.

steps.title: Set a variable for one command only
steps.text: `NAME=value command` puts `NAME` in the environment of that one command. The shell itself is not changed.

steps.title: Underneath: the environment is an array of strings
steps.text:
A program receives its environment as a second array, `envp`, next to `argv`. Each entry is `NAME=value`. Linux shows the raw bytes in `/proc/PID/environ`, separated by NUL characters.

`env -i` starts a command with an **empty** environment, so we can see exactly what the shell adds.
steps.under: `execve(path, argv, envp)` takes the environment as an explicit argument. `env` is only a program that builds an `envp` and calls `execve`.

steps.title: PATH order decides which program runs
steps.text: Bash takes the **first** match in `$PATH`. Put your own directory first and you replace a command, for better or worse. This is why a writable directory early in `PATH` is a security risk.
steps.after: `hash -r` clears bash's cache of command locations. Without it bash may keep using the old path.

quiz.q: You run `name=bob` and then `bash -c 'echo $name'`. What is printed?
quiz.explain: `name` is a shell variable and was not exported, so the child bash does not have it.

quiz.q: Which command makes `PORT` visible to every program started later from this shell?
quiz.explain: `export` adds the variable to the environment that children inherit.

quiz.q: A script changes `HOME` with `export HOME=/tmp`. Does your interactive shell's HOME change?
options: No, a child cannot change its parent's environment
Only if the script is run with sudo
quiz.explain: The script runs in a child process with its own copy of the environment.

options: Sets FOO in the shell for good
Sets FOO only in the environment of cmd
quiz.explain: Step 4: the variable exists for that one command only.

check.scenario: A script is started by cron and fails with `command not found`, but the same command works in your terminal. Give two likely causes related to this lesson.
check.answer:
1. Cron starts jobs with a **small environment**, and its `PATH` is short (often `/usr/bin:/bin`). The command lives elsewhere. Use the full path or set `PATH` in the crontab.
2. A variable you use in the terminal was set in your login shell and **not exported** (or only in `~/.bashrc`), so the cron job never gets it. Define it inside the script.

lessons.title: The order of expansions
lessons.goal:
Learn the order in which bash expands a command line and how to watch it happen.

Why it matters: the order explains puzzling results, for example why `{1..$n}` does not work and why a quoted variable is safe.

setup.note: Work in a scratch directory. Outputs will differ in PIDs and paths; the structure is the same.

steps.title: Brace expansion comes first
steps.text: `{a,b}` and `{1..3}` generate words. This happens before anything else, and it is pure text: no files are checked.
steps.after: The last line prints `{1..3}` unchanged. Brace expansion runs **before** variable expansion, so at that moment `$n` is not yet a number.

steps.title: Tilde and parameter expansion
steps.text: `~` becomes your home directory. `$var` and `${var}` become the value. `${var:-default}` uses a default when the variable is empty. `${#var}` is the length. `${var%.txt}` removes a suffix.

steps.title: Command substitution and arithmetic
steps.text: `$(cmd)` is replaced by the output of `cmd`, with trailing newlines removed. `$((expr))` is replaced by the result of an integer calculation.
steps.under: `$(...)` runs the command in a **subshell**: bash forks, the child runs `cmd` with its stdout connected to a pipe, and the parent reads the pipe.

steps.title: Word splitting uses IFS
steps.text: After expansion, **unquoted** results are split into words at the characters in `IFS` (space, tab, newline by default). Quotes prevent this.

steps.title: Pathname expansion (globbing) comes last
steps.text: Patterns `*`, `?` and `[...]` are matched against file names **after** splitting. A pattern that matches nothing stays as typed (in the default mode).

steps.title: Watch it with set -x
steps.text: `set -x` (or `bash -x`) prints each command **after expansion**, with a `+` prefix. This is the fastest way to see what bash really runs.

quiz.q: In `echo {1..$n}` with n=3, why do you NOT get `1 2 3`?
options: Brace expansion runs before variable expansion
quiz.explain: Order: brace, tilde, parameter/command/arithmetic, word splitting, globbing. `$n` is not yet expanded when braces are processed.

quiz.q: `v='a  b'`. How many arguments does `printf '[%s]\n' $v` receive?
quiz.explain: Unquoted, the value is split at blanks into `a` and `b`.

quiz.q: Which command shows the command line after expansion?

check.scenario: `for i in {1..$n}; do echo $i; done` prints `{1..3}` once. Rewrite it so it counts to n.
check.answer: Brace expansion happens before `$n` is expanded. Use a C-style loop: `for ((i=1; i<=n; i++)); do echo $i; done`, or `seq 1 "$n"`.

lessons.title: How pipes and redirection work underneath
lessons.goal:
See the system calls behind `|` and `>`: `pipe2`, `clone`, `dup2` and `execve`.

Why it matters: once you know that redirection is just `dup2` on a file descriptor, the order rules and many odd behaviours become obvious.

setup.note: Work in a scratch directory. Outputs will differ in PIDs and paths; the structure is the same.

steps.title: Trace a pipeline
steps.text: We trace `echo hi | wc -c` with the calls that build a pipeline. `-f` follows child processes. Each line starts with the process ID.

run.cmd: strace -f -o /tmp/pipe.out -e trace=pipe2,clone,dup2,dup3,execve bash -c 'echo hi | wc -c; true' > /dev/null

run.output:
3450574 execve("/usr/bin/bash", ["bash", "-c", "echo hi | wc -c; true"], 0xffffd60022e8 /* 55 vars */) = 0
3450574 pipe2([3, 4], 0)                = 0
3450575 dup3(4, 1, 0)                   = 1
3450574 <... clone resumed>, child_tidptr=0xffffab1d40f0) = 3450576
3450576 dup3(3, 0, 0)                   = 0
3450576 execve("/usr/bin/wc", ["wc", "-c"], 0xaaab01e97f40 /* 53 vars */) = 0

steps.under: Bash calls `pipe2` once: it returns two file descriptors, a read end and a write end. It forks one child per command. Each child uses `dup2` (the call is `dup3` on ARM64, same job) to put one end of the pipe on fd 1 (writer) or fd 0 (reader), closes the originals, then calls `execve`. The programs never know they are in a pipeline.
steps.after: Read the trace: one `pipe2` returns fds 3 and 4. The writer child does `dup3(4, 1)` (pipe write end becomes stdout). The reader child does `dup3(3, 0)` (read end becomes stdin) and then `execve`s `wc`. There is no `execve` for `echo`: it is a builtin, so that child runs it inside bash itself.

steps.title: A redirection is an open plus dup2
steps.text: For `> file`, the child opens the file and uses `dup2` to make fd 1 point to it. Then it runs the command. Look for `openat` and `dup2` (or `dup3` on ARM64) before the final `execve`.

run.output:
3450585 execve("/usr/bin/bash", ["bash", "-c", "/bin/echo hi > /tmp/lab/o.txt; t"...], 0xffffe9955548 /* 55 vars */) = 0
3450586 openat(AT_FDCWD, "/tmp/lab/o.txt", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0666) = 3
3450586 dup3(3, 1, 0)                   = 1
3450586 execve("/bin/echo", ["/bin/echo", "hi"], 0xaaaac2dd0f50 /* 53 vars */) = 0

steps.title: The file descriptors are visible in /proc
steps.text: Every process has a directory `/proc/PID/fd`. The links show where each descriptor points. `ls` lists its own, so we see what bash set up for it.
steps.after: In the first command `ls` writes to a file, so fd 1 points to `/tmp/lab/fd.txt`. In the second it writes into a pipe, so fd 1 shows `pipe:[number]`. The number is the pipe's inode. (Fd 0 and 2 depend on where you run this: a terminal shows `/dev/pts/N`.)

quiz.q: Which system call creates the two ends of a pipe?
quiz.explain: `pipe2` (or `pipe`) returns a read fd and a write fd.

options: Makes fd 1 refer to the same open file as fd
quiz.explain: After dup2, descriptor 1 points to the same open file description as `fd`.

quiz.q: When does the redirection happen, relative to `execve` of the command?
quiz.explain: The child sets up descriptors, then calls `execve`. The new program inherits them.

check.scenario: Why can `echo hi | read v; echo $v` print nothing in bash?
check.answer: Each command of a pipeline runs in its own child process. `read v` sets `v` in a child, which exits when the pipeline ends. The parent shell never gets the variable. Use `read v < <(echo hi)` or a here-string `read v <<< hi`.

interview.q: What happens, in order, when you type `ls *.txt` and press Enter?
interview.a:
1. Bash splits the line into words.
2. It expands the words (here: the `*.txt` glob becomes the matching file names).
3. It looks for the command: function, builtin, then each directory in `$PATH`.
4. It forks a child process.
5. The child sets up redirections and calls `execve` with the expanded words as `argv`.
6. Bash waits for the child and stores its exit code in `$?`.

See [the lesson](#/lesson/1/how-bash-runs-a-command/8).

interview.q: What is the difference between `cmd > f 2>&1` and `cmd 2>&1 > f`?
interview.a: Redirections are applied left to right. In the first, stdout goes to `f`, then stderr is pointed at where stdout is now (`f`). In the second, stderr is pointed at the terminal first, then only stdout goes to `f`, so errors still show on the terminal. See [step 10](#/lesson/1/how-bash-runs-a-command/10).

interview.q: Why is `cd` a shell builtin and not a program?
interview.a: The current directory belongs to a process. A program started by the shell is a child process, so changing its directory would not affect the shell. Only a builtin runs inside the shell process.

interview.q: What do exit codes 126 and 127 mean?
interview.a: 127: command not found. 126: the file was found but could not be executed (for example, no execute permission).

interview.q: A script breaks on file names with spaces. What is the usual cause and fix?
interview.a: An unquoted expansion was split into several words. Quote it: `"$var"`. See [step 5](#/lesson/1/how-bash-runs-a-command/5).

interview.q: What is the difference between a shell variable and an environment variable?
interview.a: A shell variable exists only in the shell process. An environment variable has been exported, so it is copied into the environment of every child started afterwards. See [the lesson](#/lesson/1/environment-and-path).

interview.q: In which order does bash expand a command line?
interview.a: Brace expansion, tilde expansion, parameter/variable, command substitution and arithmetic (left to right), word splitting, pathname expansion (globbing), then quote removal. See [the lesson](#/lesson/1/expansion-order).

Bash calls `pipe2`, forks two children, and each child uses `dup2` to put one end of the pipe on its stdout or stdin before `execve`. Both run at the same time. See [the trace](#/lesson/1/pipes-underneath).

interview.q: Why do variables set in a `while read` loop at the end of a pipe disappear?
interview.a: The loop runs in a child process (a subshell). When it ends, its variables are gone. Feed the loop with `< <(cmd)` or a file redirect so it runs in the current shell.

interview.q: Why does `rm $f` break on a name with spaces?
interview.a: The unquoted expansion is split into words. Quote it: `rm "$f"`.

glossary.def: The array of argument strings a program receives when it starts. Index 0 is the program name.
A command implemented inside the shell itself, not a file on disk. Example: cd.
The number a process returns when it ends. 0 means success. Bash stores it in $?.
Expansion of patterns such as *.txt into matching file names. Done by the shell before the program runs.
A colon-separated list of directories the shell searches for programs whose name has no slash.
Using single quotes, double quotes or a backslash to stop or limit shell expansion.
Changing where a standard file descriptor (0, 1, 2) points before a command runs.
Cutting the result of an unquoted expansion into separate words at blanks.
A NAME=value string passed to a process in its envp array. Children inherit a copy.
Generation of words from {a,b} or {1..3}. It is the first expansion and ignores files.
Internal Field Separator: the characters at which bash splits unquoted expansion results. Default: space, tab, newline.
$(cmd): replaced by the output of cmd, which runs in a subshell.
A child copy of the shell process that runs part of a command line, such as a pipeline stage or $(...).
System call that makes one file descriptor refer to the same open file as another. The basis of redirection.
A kernel buffer with a read end and a write end, created by pipe2. Connects stdout of one process to stdin of another.

commands.desc: Show every way NAME can be run (alias, builtin, file).
Print the PATH directories, one per line.
Print the exit code of the last command.
Send stdout and stderr to a file.
Send only stderr to a file.
Show how bash forks and execs a command.
Set a variable and put it in the environment of children.
Run cmd with an empty environment plus NAME.
Use a default when var is empty.
Run a script printing each command after expansion.
Show the open file descriptors of the current process.
Clear bash's cache of command locations.
